m5-6-q1.s: With PVST+, the bridge ID's priority field is split into a 4-bit priority and a 12-bit **extended system ID**, which holds the **VLAN ID**. That gives every VLAN its own bridge ID while using the same MAC address.

m5-6-q2.s: When STP starts, **every switch assumes it is the root** and sends BPDUs with its own bridge ID as the root ID. When a switch hears a lower (better) ID, it stops claiming root and passes along the better one. Ports are chosen and blocked only after that.

m5-6-q3.s: Each non-root switch picks one **root port**: the port with the **lowest total path cost to the root bridge**.
x: A designated port is the best port *on a segment*, not the switch's best path to the root.
Alternate ports are backups that are blocking or discarding.

m5-6-q4.s: A port that connects only to end devices is an **edge port**. On Cisco switches you set this with **PortFast**, so the port skips listening/learning and starts forwarding right away.

m5-6-q5.s: Bridge ID = **bridge priority** (4 bits) + **extended system ID** (12 bits, the VLAN) + **MAC address** (48 bits). Lowest BID wins the root election.

m5-6-q6.s:
STP flavours:
**STP (802.1D)** – one tree for all VLANs, slow.
**PVST+** – Cisco, one 802.1D tree per VLAN.
**RSTP (802.1w)** – rapid convergence, one tree.
**Rapid PVST+** – Cisco, one RSTP tree per VLAN.
**MSTP/MST (802.1s)** – maps groups of VLANs to a small number of RSTP instances.

m5-6-q7.s: MAC addresses are learned in the **learning** and **forwarding** states. BPDUs are processed in blocking, listening, learning and forwarding, but only learning and forwarding do both.
x: Listening and blocking process BPDUs but don't learn MAC addresses.
Disabled ports do nothing.

m5-6-q8.s: If every switch keeps the default priority (32768 + VLAN ID), the tie is broken by the **lowest MAC address**, which then becomes the root bridge. STP doesn't look at IP addresses.

m5-6-q9.s:
Matching tips:
**PVST+** – Cisco, per-VLAN 802.1D.
**Rapid PVST+** – Cisco, per-VLAN RSTP.
**RSTP** – IEEE 802.1w, fast convergence.
**MSTP** – IEEE 802.1s, VLANs mapped to instances.
Check the image for the exact pairing.

m5-6-q10.s: Only **root ports** and **designated ports** forward. Alternate (blocked) ports discard, and disabled ports are shut down.

m5-6-q11.s: STP lets you build **redundant links** without loops. It **blocks the extra paths** and re-enables them if the active path fails.
x: Aggregating links is EtherChannel.
Shrinking failure domains is a design goal, not STP's job.

m5-6-q12.s: Spanning tree is **on by default** on Cisco switches (PVST+). It exists *because* Ethernet frames have **no TTL**, so a loop would circulate frames forever.
x: Discovering neighbor devices is CDP/LLDP.
STP doesn't stop broadcasts; it only removes the loops they could travel around.

m5-6-q13.s: Original **IEEE 802.1D** runs **one spanning tree for all VLANs**: one root bridge, so every VLAN takes the same path.
x: PVST+ and Rapid PVST+ run one tree per VLAN.
MST groups VLANs into several instances.

m5-6-q14.s: STP's job is to **prevent Layer 2 loops**, and the broadcast storms and MAC table instability they cause, by keeping exactly one active path.
x: Routing loops are handled by routing protocols, not STP.
Collision and broadcast domains are set by switches, routers and VLANs.

m5-6-q15.s: The root port is chosen by the **lowest root path cost**. Ties are broken by the lowest sender bridge ID, then the lowest port ID.

m5-6-q16.s: All priorities are equal, so the **lowest MAC address** decides. **S2** has the lowest MAC, so it becomes the root bridge.

m5-6-q17.s: Without STP, redundant links cause loops: **broadcasts circulate forever** (a broadcast storm), and the same MAC is seen on different ports, so the **MAC table keeps changing**. Hosts can also receive duplicate unicast frames.

m5-6-q18.s: Priority must be a **multiple of 4096** from 0 to 61440. The default is 32768. Setting one switch **lower**, such as **28672**, makes it the root.
x: 1 and 34816 aren't multiples of 4096.
32768 is the default and would only tie.
61440 makes it the *least* likely root.

m5-6-q19.s: One EtherChannel must connect the **same two devices**: switch to switch, or switch to an EtherChannel-capable server. You can't bundle links that go to two different switches.
x: Splitting one bundle across two chassis needs special stacking/multichassis features, which are outside this course.

m5-6-q20.s: **PAgP is Cisco-proprietary**. **LACP (IEEE 802.3ad)** is the open standard and works with other vendors.
x: PAgP doesn't require an even number of links or more links than LACP.
The bundle counts as one STP port, so fewer STP ports, not more.

m5-6-q21.s: Ports in a bundle must match on **speed**, **duplex** and **VLAN settings** (the same access VLAN, or trunk mode with the same allowed VLANs and native VLAN).
x: The ports don't have to be next to each other on the switch.

m5-6-q22.s: The output shows the bundle was negotiated with **PAgP**, the **Cisco-proprietary** protocol. LACP is the open-standard alternative.

m5-6-q23.s: PAgP bundles form only when the ports match on **speed/duplex** and **VLAN information**. The PAgP modes only need to be compatible (desirable/auto), not identical.
x: Port IDs and MAC addresses are always different and don't need to match.

m5-6-q24.s: Mode **on** forces a bundle *without* any negotiation protocol, so it only works if the other side is also **on**. SW2 is using PAgP **desirable**, which never gets a reply, so the EtherChannel **fails**.

m5-6-q25.s: Compatible pairs: PAgP **desirable–desirable** or **desirable–auto**; LACP **active–active** or **active–passive**; **on–on**. SW1 is in **auto**, so SW2 must be **desirable**.

m5-6-q26.s: An EtherChannel is one logical link. If one member fails, the **others keep carrying traffic** (load-balanced), and STP doesn't recalculate.

m5-6-q27.s: **auto** (PAgP) only responds; it never starts negotiation. The other side must actively ask, which is **desirable**.
x: active and passive are LACP modes and don't talk to PAgP.

m5-6-q28.s: **LACP** (IEEE 802.3ad) is the **open-standard** way to bundle ports into one logical link.
x: PAgP is Cisco-proprietary.
DTP negotiates trunks.
Multilink PPP bundles serial links.

m5-6-q29.s: For a trunking EtherChannel, **all member ports must allow the same VLANs** (and use the same native VLAN). Otherwise the bundle won't form.
x: Ports don't need to be contiguous or on the same module.
Trunk ports don't get an access VLAN number.

m5-6-q30.s: LACP **negotiates** the bundle between directly connected switches, so mismatches are caught. Because it's an open standard, it also works with **other vendors' devices**.
x: You can't mix Fast Ethernet and Gigabit ports in one bundle.

m5-6-q31.s: A **designated port** is the best port on a segment toward the root. It isn't the switch's root port, but it **forwards traffic**. (All ports on the root bridge are designated.)

m5-6-q32.s: EtherChannel treats the bundle as **one logical link**, so STP doesn't block members. You also configure **one port-channel interface**, which keeps every member configured consistently.
x: Load balancing happens inside one bundle, not between bundles.
It uses existing ports; no upgraded links are needed.

m5-6-q33.s: S1 is the root, so its port **B is designated**. **C and D** are the best paths to the root on their switches, so they're **root ports**. **A** is a redundant path in RSTP's **alternate** role, which is discarding.

m5-6-q34.s: **EtherChannel** bundles several physical uplinks into one logical link for more bandwidth, and STP doesn't block any of them.
x: Trunking carries VLANs but doesn't add bandwidth.
HSRP provides gateway redundancy.
PortFast speeds up edge ports.

m5-6-q35.s: PAgP **auto** waits to be asked, so S2 must be **desirable** to start the negotiation.

m5-6-q36.s: On SW1, Gi0/2 is already in channel-group 1, but **Gi0/1 is missing** from it. Add Gi0/1 to the same group with a compatible mode.

m5-6-q37.s: Priority goes in steps of 4096, and **lower is better**. The **highest valid value, 61440**, makes a switch the *least* likely root.
x: 65535 isn't a valid priority.

m5-6-q38.s: PVST+ learns MAC addresses in the **learning** and **forwarding** states. Blocking and listening only process BPDUs.

m5-6-q39.s: The **root port** is the switch's port with the **lowest cost to the root bridge**. Every non-root switch has exactly one.

m5-6-q40.s: The **root port** is the port closest to the root bridge by total path cost.

m5-6-q42.s: The **extended system ID** is the 12-bit part of the bridge ID that holds the **VLAN ID**.

m5-6-q43.s: Every STP path cost is measured **to the root bridge**. It is the reference point of the tree.

m5-6-q44.s: **Bridge priority** (default **32768**) is compared first in the root election. The MAC address breaks ties.

m5-6-q45.s: **Trunk ports can be bundled**. All members then have to be trunks with the same allowed VLANs and native VLAN.
x: EtherChannel can be Layer 2 or Layer 3.
PAgP is one of its negotiation protocols.
Up to 8 active links (16 with LACP standby), not 10.

m5-6-q46.s: In `show etherchannel summary`, **(SD)** means a Layer 2 port-channel (S) that is **down** (D). The members show as stand-alone, so **the EtherChannel is not working**.

m5-6-q47.s: EtherChannel bundles **several identical physical links into one logical link** between two switches (or a switch and a server).
x: You can't mix speeds.
Up to 8 active links, not 4.

m5-6-q48.s: PAgP modes **desirable** (actively negotiates) and **auto** (responds) both negotiate. **on** forces the channel with no negotiation. active and passive belong to LACP.

m5-6-q49.s: Mode **on** on both ends forms the EtherChannel **without sending PAgP or LACP packets**.
x: desirable and active/passive send negotiation traffic.
auto–auto never forms a channel.

m5-6-q50.s: The member trunks on S1 and S2 allow **different VLAN ranges**. Every member must have the same allowed VLAN list, or the bundle won't form.

m5-6-q51.s: **on** forces the port into the channel **without exchanging PAgP or LACP packets**.

m5-6-q52.s: EtherChannel can load-balance by **source/destination MAC** or **source/destination IP** (and, on some platforms, by port numbers). The method is set with `port-channel load-balance`.

m5-6-q53.s: **MST** maps many VLANs into a few **RSTP instances** (up to 16 in Cisco's implementation), and it supports PortFast, BPDU guard, root guard and so on.

m5-6-q54.s: In a broadcast storm, looping broadcasts use up all the bandwidth and CPU. The switches can't keep up, so **new traffic is dropped**.

m5-6-q55.s: STP is needed whenever there are **redundant Layer 2 links** or **multiple switches added to remove single points of failure**, because both create loops.
x: Static and dynamic routing are Layer 3.
VLANs limit broadcasts but don't stop loops.

m5-6-q56.s: If one member of a 4-link EtherChannel goes down, **the EtherChannel stays up** on the remaining links. STP still sees one logical link, so it doesn't recalculate.
